newsitem.title: UK: Copper skittish on LME, ends with pared gains.
newsitem.headline: Copper skittish on LME, ends with pared gains.

text.p: Copper prices whipsawed during Thursday LME trading, moving sharply at times either side of overnight levels before ending the session steadier, but down from highs just above $1,950.

Traders said today's movements were typical of a market that has moved up by some $100 in two days, but is largely uncertain. Key upside levels were defended, with some bank sales preventing the market running higher on option covering, leaving the next major move uncertain.
"At the moment it could go either way - up to $1,970 or back down to $1,900. Fundamentals are finely balanced with the market veering between backwardation and contango," one said.

Today's latest developments in the Sumitomo Corp scandal did not influence the market to any great extent. Sumitomo said its losses in 10 years of unauthorised trading by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka were $2.6 billion, not the $1.8 billion originally reported. Most of its uncovered poisitions have now been liquidated.
"You would hardly expect them (Sumitomo) to say they had positions left just after they up the losses," another trader said.
Copper prices ended the kerb at $1,936, up $11 a tonne from Wednesday, but down from a $1,953 peak. Stocks are seen falling tomorrow, traders said.

Aluminium largely fluctuated in line with copper, but price movements were kept to a minimum as the market looked to consolidate after hitting 2-1/4 year lows at the beginning of the week, traders said.

LME stocks are seen rising tomorrow, while IPAI production data for August is expected to show that output is rising, although there is likely to be little market reaction as these figures continue current trends. Aluminium concluded the kerb at $1,428, a $5 loss.
Nickel trading was jerky throughout, with prices largely dependant on copper for direction, although there is an undercurrent of support from the ongoing Inco dispute.
However, a mid-afternoon rally stalled at the technical hurdle of $7,500, and with stocks seen rising on Friday last kerb trade was at $7,390, down $60 from Wednesday.
Zinc prices settled back into the $1,030/40 band, having faltered above the upper end of that range earlier in the session. Last business was at $1,035.50, down $5.50 from yesterday.

Lead was partially bolstered by short-covering, with short-term technicals oversold, although there was not enough impetus to drive prices back above $800. By the end of the kerb prices had settled at $787, down just $1 from the previous kerb.

Tin business was disappointing, with the market gradually losing ground and heading back towards the $6,100 level. Developments regarding the ATPC are not exciting the market at present, they said. Last trade was at $6,119, a $21 loss from the previous kerb.
Alloy was quiet throughout the day, closing at $1,240/45 a tonne, against an overnight $1,241. --Martin Hayes, London newsroom 44 171 542 8080
